sentences.text: The train pulled away from the tiny station, and Wren was alone on the platform.
Fellwick was smaller than she had expected.
Two streets, a bakery, a post office that had a cat sleeping in the window, and a hill.
At the top of the hill was the house she had come to stay in for the summer.
She had never met her Great-Aunt Marlow.
Her mother had said only that Aunt Marlow was 'a bit unusual, but perfectly kind,' which Wren had noticed was the sort of thing grown-ups said when they meant something else entirely.
The door opened before Wren could knock.
Great-Aunt Marlow was tall and thin, with white hair pinned up in a knot and glasses on a chain around her neck.
She smelled of lavender and old paper.
"You must be Wren," she said, looking down at her.
"You look exactly like your mother did at your age.
Come in, come in.
Mind the umbrella stand."
Wren stepped inside, and stopped.
Every wall was covered in clocks.
Grandfather clocks stood in the corners.
Cuckoo clocks hung by the windows.
Small brass clocks sat on the mantel, next to porcelain clocks shaped like cats.
There were clocks with painted faces, clocks with glass fronts, clocks with no numbers at all — only tiny stars where the numbers should have been.
And every single one of them was ticking.
"They were my father's," said Great-Aunt Marlow, hanging Wren's coat on a hook shaped like a hand.
"And his father's before him.
Every clock in this house has a story.
Some of the stories are quite good."
She turned and looked at Wren over the top of her glasses.
"You can wander wherever you like, my dear.
Open any door.
Read any book.
There is only one rule."
Wren waited.
"If any of the clocks strikes thirteen," said Great-Aunt Marlow, "do not look behind you."
It was the sort of rule you smile at politely and then forget.
Wren smiled politely.
Great-Aunt Marlow went off to the kitchen to put the kettle on, and Wren wandered down the hall by herself, counting clocks.
She was up to twenty-eight when she stopped.
There was one clock she had missed.
It was small and made of dark wood, hanging just above a doorway at the end of the hall.
It looked ordinary in every way except one.
Its hands were moving backwards.
Wren watched it for a long minute.
The second hand crawled from the seven to the six, from the six to the five, from the five to the four.
Not fast.
Not slow.
Just backwards, as if it had somewhere to be in yesterday.
"That one belonged to my great-grandfather," said Great-Aunt Marlow, appearing suddenly at Wren's elbow with a cup of tea.
"He was a clockmaker, and a fool.
Come along.
Your room is up the stairs, first on the left.
There is a book about beetles on the pillow if you would like something to read."
That night, Wren lay in bed and listened.
The clocks did not tick in unison.
They ticked in a kind of soft rain — some fast, some slow, some deep and heavy like footsteps, some light as fingertips on a table.
Wren found it strangely restful, and she was almost asleep when the first clock began to strike midnight.
She counted along in her head.
One.
Two.
Three.
Four.
Five.
Six.
Seven.
Eight.
Nine.
Ten.
Eleven.
Twelve.
There was a pause.
Then, from somewhere down the hall, one more clock struck.
Just once.
Softly.
Thirteen.
